The breast engorgement with con- sequent discomfort and galactorrhoea triggered by prolac- tin secretion post partum can be problematic in women who choose not to breast feed or are unable to do so. Non- steroidal or synthetic oestrogens were historically used to suppress lactation in such women, but this use is now con- sidered inappropriate because of an increased risk of thromboembolism. Bromocriptine is a potent inhibitor of prolactin secretion: it has been given post partum in short treatment courses (about 14 days) to suppress lactation. However, it has also been associated with severe adverse effects, and its use for lactation suppression is no longer advocated in a number of countries. Other dopaminergics with similar actions such as cabergoline, lisuride, metergo- line, and quinagolide have also been used to suppress lac- tation. Although it has been suggested that cabergoline, which is generally better tolerated than bromocriptine, may be a better choice for lactation inhibition,1 the same general objections as for bromocriptine apply to all these drugs. A study in HIV-infected women requiring lactation suppression (in order to prevent mother-to-child transmis- sion from breast milk) found that a combined oral contra- ceptive was as effective as bromocriptine.2 Non-pharma- cological methods include warm showers to induce milk leakage and reduce pressure, ice packs to reduce local pain and swelling, and a well fitting supportive brassiere. The removal of just enough milk to reduce the pressure but not enough to empty the breasts may help to reduce milk pro- duction gradually. Active treatments including mild analgesics such as ibuprofen or paracetamol are also advo- cated.3 However, a review4 noted that few non-pharmaco- logical methods were well evaluated, and that mild analge- sia might not be enough to prevent the considerable pain experienced by many women. Lactation induction. Drug therapy has sometimes been used to help stimulate lactation, although mechanical stim- ulation of the nipple remains the primary method.5 Dopamine antagonists, of which metoclopramide has been the most widely used, can produce modest increases in breast milk production but carry a risk of adverse effects including dystonias. If used, such therapy should be limit- ed to 1 or 2 weeks; there has also been some concern about the presence of these drugs in breast milk.5,6 The efficacy of metoclopramide in stimulating lactation in women with preterm deliveries has been questioned by a controlled study.7 Domperidone has also been reported to increase milk production,6,8 and may cause fewer adverse central effects than metoclopramide.
